description: Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is a culinary masterpiece, a rich and complex sauce with a deep, dark hue. This traditional Mexican dish masterfully blends a symphony of chiles, spices, nuts, and chocolate to create an unforgettable flavor experience. Perfect for special occasions, it transforms simple chicken or turkey into an extraordinary meal.

instructions.title: Toast Chiles and Rehydrate
instructions.text: Lightly toast the dried ancho, mulato, and pasilla chiles in a dry pan over medium heat for 2-3 minutes until fragrant. Be careful not to burn them. Immediately transfer the toasted chiles to a bowl, cover with hot water, and let them rehydrate for 15-20 minutes until soft. Drain and set aside, reserving some soaking liquid.

instructions.title: Toast Nuts, Seeds, and Aromatics
instructions.text: In the same dry pan, toast the almonds, peanuts, sesame seeds, and pumpkin seeds separately until lightly golden and fragrant, about 1-2 minutes each. Set aside. In a little oil, lightly fry the garlic, onion, roasted tomatoes, roasted tomatillos, fried tortillas, fried plantain, and raisins until softened and slightly caramelized. Add the cinnamon stick, cloves, peppercorns, cumin seeds, and oregano to the pan and toast for 30 seconds.

instructions.title: Blend the Mole Paste
instructions.text: Combine the rehydrated chiles, toasted nuts and seeds, fried aromatics, and spices in a blender. Add 2 cups of hot chicken broth and blend until a very smooth paste forms. If needed, add a little more broth or reserved chile soaking liquid to achieve a smooth consistency. Strain the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl, pressing firmly to extract all liquid and discarding any solids.

instructions.title: Fry the Mole Paste
instructions.text: Heat the lard or vegetable oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Once hot, carefully pour in the strained mole paste. Cook, stirring constantly, for about 8-10 minutes. This frying process is crucial for deepening the flavor and color of the mole, preventing it from tasting raw. Be careful as it may splatter.

instructions.title: Simmer and Season
instructions.text: Gradually stir in the remaining hot chicken broth, about 1 cup at a time, until the mole reaches your desired consistency. It should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Add the chopped Mexican chocolate and stir until it is completely melted and incorporated. Season with salt to taste. Reduce heat to low and simmer for at least 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, allowing the flavors to meld. If the mole becomes too thick, add a little more broth.

instructions.title: Serve and Enjoy
instructions.text: Serve the Mole Negro hot over cooked chicken pieces. Garnish with a sprinkle of sesame seeds, if desired. It pairs wonderfully with white rice and warm corn tortillas. This rich sauce is also excellent with turkey or pork.

tips: To achieve the deepest color and flavor, ensure your chiles are thoroughly toasted but not burnt before rehydrating. A comal or dry skillet works best.
Mexican chocolate is essential for its unique blend of cacao, sugar, and cinnamon. Do not substitute with regular baking chocolate, as it will alter the authentic flavor profile.
Mole freezes beautifully! Make a large batch and store portions in airtight containers for up to 3 months. Thaw and reheat gently, adding a splash of broth if needed.
article:
The world of Mexican Dinner Recipes is vast and vibrant, but few dishes command the respect and admiration given to mole. Among the pantheon of moles, none is perhaps as revered and complex as **Oaxacan Black Mole**, or Mole Negro. This isn't just a sauce; it's a culinary masterpiece, a symphony of flavors that tells the story of Oaxaca, its rich history, and its deep connection to the earth. Often reserved for special occasions and celebrations, making Mole Negro from scratch is a labor of love, a meditative process that yields one of the most unforgettable dining experiences imaginable.

## What is Oaxacan Black Mole (Mole Negro)?

**Oaxacan Black Mole** is the most celebrated of Oaxaca’s "seven moles," renowned for its deep, almost mystical dark color and incredibly intricate flavor profile. Originating in the southern Mexican state of Oaxaca, known as the "Land of Seven Moles," Mole Negro stands out for its extraordinary list of ingredients—often exceeding 20 or even 30—and the meticulous process required to transform them into a cohesive, velvety sauce.

At its heart, Mole Negro is a delicate balance of sweet, savory, spicy, and earthy notes. It derives its characteristic darkness from a specific blend of dried chiles, primarily the rare chilhuacle negro, alongside mulato, pasilla, and ancho chiles, which are often toasted to the point of charring. Beyond the chiles, the ingredient list reads like an ancient apothecary: nuts, seeds, spices, fruits, vegetables, and, crucially, Mexican chocolate. Each component is individually toasted, fried, or rehydrated before being ground into a fine paste, then slowly simmered for hours. The result is a thick, rich, and intensely flavored sauce that is smoky, subtly sweet, a little spicy, and profoundly complex, offering a taste of Mexico's culinary soul.

## Ingredients for Authentic Mole Negro

Preparing an authentic Mole Negro requires a commitment to sourcing a diverse range of ingredients, each playing a vital role in the final flavor. While the exact proportions can vary by family recipe, these are the essential components:

*   **Dried Chiles (approx. 20-25 total):**
    *   10-12 Mulato chiles (for dark color and mild fruitiness)
    *   8-10 Pasilla Oaxaca chiles (for smokiness and medium heat)
    *   5-6 Ancho chiles (for deep color and fruity notes)
    *   *Optional but traditional:* 2-3 Chilhuacle Negro chiles (if available, for unparalleled complexity and deep black color; these are rare and expensive)
*   **Nuts & Seeds:** 1/2 cup almonds, 1/4 cup peanuts, 1/4 cup sesame seeds, 2 tbsp pumpkin seeds
*   **Spices:** 1/2 tsp whole black peppercorns, 1/4 tsp whole cloves, 1 small stick true cinnamon (Canela), 1/2 tsp cumin seeds, 1/4 tsp anise seeds, 1/2 tsp dried oregano, 1/4 tsp dried thyme, 1/4 tsp marjoram
*   **Fruits:** 1 ripe plantain (sliced), 1/4 cup raisins
*   **Vegetables:** 2 medium tomatoes (roughly chopped), 1 small tomatillo (husked), 1/2 medium white onion (roughly chopped), 4-5 cloves garlic
*   **Thickeners/Enrichers:** 2 slices stale bread (or 2 corn tortillas, fried until crisp)
*   **Fat:** 1/4 cup lard or vegetable oil
*   **Broth:** 4-6 cups chicken broth (or vegetable broth for a vegetarian version)
*   **Chocolate:** 1.5-2 ounces Mexican chocolate (preferably unsweetened or very dark)
*   **Seasoning:** Salt to taste, a pinch of sugar (optional, to balance bitterness)

## Step-by-Step Instructions to Make Oaxacan Black Mole

Making **Oaxacan Black Mole** is a journey, not a sprint. Patience and attention to detail are your best tools.

1.  **Prepare the Chiles:** Carefully toast the chiles on a comal or dry skillet over medium heat until aromatic and slightly pliable, being careful not to burn them (this takes 30-60 seconds per side). Stem and seed the chiles. Rehydrate them by soaking in hot water for 20-30 minutes until soft. Drain, reserving some soaking liquid.
2.  **Toast Nuts and Seeds:** In a clean, dry skillet, toast the almonds, peanuts, sesame seeds, and pumpkin seeds separately until lightly golden and fragrant. Set aside.
3.  **Fry Aromatics and Thickeners:** Heat the lard or oil in a large pot or deep skillet. Fry the onion, garlic, tomatoes, and tomatillo until softened and slightly browned. Remove. In the same fat, fry the plantain slices and raisins until golden. Fry the stale bread or tortillas until crisp.
4.  **Grind Spices:** In a spice grinder or molcajete, grind the peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon, cumin, anise, oregano, thyme, and marjoram to a fine powder.
5.  **Blend Everything:** Combine the rehydrated chiles, toasted nuts and seeds, fried vegetables and fruits, fried bread/tortillas, and ground spices in a high-speed blender. Add 2 cups of chicken broth and blend until incredibly smooth. This may require working in batches and adding more broth or reserved chile soaking liquid as needed to achieve a thick, pourable paste. Strain the paste through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl, pressing down on the solids to extract all liquid. Discard any remaining fibrous material.
6.  **Sauté the Mole Paste:** In a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, heat a fresh tablespoon of lard or oil over medium heat. Carefully add the strained mole paste. This step is crucial for developing the deep flavor. Cook, stirring constantly, for at least 20-30 minutes, or until the paste darkens further and thickens considerably, becoming glossy and aromatic. It will spit and splatter, so be careful.
7.  **Simmer and Finish:** Gradually stir in the remaining chicken broth, a cup at a time, bringing the mole to a gentle simmer after each addition. Continue to simmer the mole for at least 1-2 hours, stirring occasionally, allowing the flavors to meld and deepen. The mole should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
8.  **Add Chocolate and Season:** In the last 15 minutes of simmering, stir in the Mexican chocolate until fully melted and incorporated. Season with salt to taste and add a pinch of sugar if needed to balance any bitterness or acidity. The mole should have a balanced sweet, savory, and spicy profile.

## Pro Tips for the Best Oaxacan Black Mole

Crafting the perfect **Oaxacan Black Mole** is an art, and these tips will help you achieve a truly exceptional result:

*   **Patience is Paramount:** This is not a quick dish. Each step, from toasting to simmering, requires time and attention. Rushing will compromise the depth of flavor. Embrace the process!
*   **Ingredient Quality Matters:** Seek out the best quality dried chiles you can find. If chilhuacle negro chiles are unavailable, don't despair; a good blend of mulato, pasilla, and ancho will still yield a delicious mole. Freshly toasted nuts and spices make a huge difference.
*   **Don't Burn the Chiles:** When toasting chiles, a fine line exists between aromatic and burnt. Burnt chiles will impart a bitter flavor that can ruin your mole. Toast them quickly until fragrant and slightly pliable.
*   **Strain, Strain, Strain:** Straining the blended paste is critical for achieving the silky-smooth texture characteristic of authentic Mole Negro. Don't skip this step, even if it's tedious.
*   **The Sauté is Key:** The long sautéing of the mole paste in fat (the "freír") is essential for developing the deep, rich color and complex flavors. It’s when the raw flavors transform into something truly magical.
*   **Make Ahead and Freeze:** Mole Negro actually improves in flavor after a day or two, allowing the ingredients to meld further. It also freezes beautifully for up to several months, making it an ideal candidate for batch cooking.

## Serving Suggestions for Mole Negro

**Oaxacan Black Mole** is traditionally served as a luxurious sauce over poultry, most commonly shredded chicken or turkey. The rich, complex flavors of the mole beautifully complement the mildness of the meat.

*   **Classic Pairing:** Serve generous portions of the mole over cooked chicken or turkey pieces (thighs, breasts, or shredded meat).
*   **Accompaniments:** Always accompany with warm corn tortillas (freshly made if possible) for scooping up every last drop, and fluffy white rice to soak up the sauce.
*   **Garnishes:** A sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds, a few slivers of fresh red onion, or a sprig of cilantro add a touch of freshness and visual appeal.
*   **Beyond Poultry:** While traditional, mole can also be used in creative ways. It makes an incredible filling for enchiladas or tamales, can be drizzled over roasted pork or even grilled vegetables for a vegetarian main course. Some even enjoy it for breakfast over fried eggs!

## Variations and Substitutions for Black Mole

While the pursuit of an authentic **Oaxacan Black Mole** is rewarding, practical considerations sometimes necessitate variations or substitutions.

*   **Chile Substitutions:** The rare chilhuacle negro is often difficult to find outside of Oaxaca. If you can't source them, increase the amounts of mulato, pasilla Oaxaca, and ancho chiles. Some recipes suggest adding a small amount of dark cocoa powder (unsweetened) or charring some tortillas to deepen the color if chilhuacle is absent.
*   **Simplified Versions:** For those new to mole-making or short on time, some Mexican grocery stores offer high-quality mole pastes or concentrates. While not a substitute for homemade, they provide a good starting point for a quicker mole experience. You would typically dilute these pastes with broth and add your own touch of chocolate and seasoning.
*   **Dietary Adjustments:** For a vegetarian or vegan version, simply substitute chicken broth with vegetable broth and use vegetable oil instead of lard. Ensure your Mexican chocolate is dairy-free if following a strict vegan diet.
*   **Other Moles:** Remember that Oaxaca is home to seven moles! If black mole seems too daunting, consider trying a Mole Coloradito (reddish-brown, often sweeter) or a bright, herbaceous Mole Verde. Each offers a unique flavor profile and can be an excellent introduction to the diverse world of Mexican Dinner Recipes.

Embracing the challenge of making Mole Negro is a culinary adventure that connects you to centuries of Mexican tradition. It's a dish that truly embodies the concept of slow food, rewarding your patience with unparalleled depth and flavor.
